unit.title: Seasons and adaptations
unit.blurb: Why we have days, years and seasons, and how living things are adapted to survive.

O1.t: Describe how the Earth spins on a tilted axis (day and night) and orbits the Sun (a year).

O2.t: Explain how the tilt of the Earth causes the seasons, and describe seasonal changes, including near the equator.

O3.t: Use shadow measurements to track the height of the Sun through the year.

O4.t: Describe how plants and animals are adapted to their environments and to seasonal changes.

O5.t: Describe adaptations of predators and prey, including camouflage and warning colours.

captions: Hello, space travellers! Fasten your seatbelts, because you are moving right now!
This is lesson 6.1: the Earth moving around the Sun.
Guess what? You are riding on a giant spaceship called Earth.
It spins round and round, and it zooms around the Sun at about thirty kilometres every second!
But everything moves with you, so you do not feel a thing.
The Earth spins on its axis once every twenty-four hours. That gives us day and night.
And the Earth travels around the Sun once every three hundred and sixty-five days. That journey is one year. Its path is called an orbit.
Pause and think. How long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun?
Every time you have a birthday…
…you and the Earth have travelled one whole lap around the Sun.
So if you are ten years old, you have done ten laps. That is about nine billion kilometres. Happy birthday, space traveller!
Here is something very important. The Earth's axis is not straight up. It is tilted, like a spinning top leaning over.
As the Earth goes around the Sun, first one half and then the other half leans towards the Sun. This tilt gives us the seasons.
Did you know? A year is really about three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter days.
So every four years, we add an extra day to the calendar: the twenty-ninth of February. That is a leap year!
Your turn. What causes day and night?
Let's make a model.
In a dark room, shine a torch, the Sun, at a globe, the Earth.
Slowly spin the globe. Which countries have day, and which have night?
Then walk the globe all the way around the torch. That is one year!
Let's remember.
The Earth spins on its axis, giving us day and night.
One spin takes twenty-four hours.
One orbit around the Sun takes a year.
And the Earth's axis is tilted.
Stellar work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, weather watchers! Grab your sun hat… or your scarf!
This is lesson 6.2: seasonal changes.
In many countries, the year has four seasons. In spring, new leaves and flowers grow.
Summer is hot, with long days.
In autumn, it gets cooler, and many trees drop their leaves.
Winter is cold, with short days and long nights.
When your half of the Earth leans towards the Sun, it is summer.
The Sun climbs high in the sky, its light is stronger, and the days are long.
When your half leans away, it is winter. The Sun stays low, and the days are short.
Pause and think. In summer, is the Sun high or low in the sky?
Here is a fun fact about the tilt. When the north half of the Earth has winter…
…the south half has summer! So December is winter in the United Kingdom, but summer in Australia.
Some families in Australia eat their Christmas lunch on the beach!
Not every place has four seasons. Near the equator, like in Vietnam's south or Singapore, it is warm all year.
Instead, there is a wet season, with lots of rain…
…and a dry season, with less rain.
Joke time! What season is it when you are on a trampoline?
Spring time!
Your turn. When it is summer in the northern half of the Earth, what season is it in the southern half?
Let's track the Sun through the seasons.
Push a stick into the ground in a sunny place, and measure its shadow at midday.
Measure it again at midday once every month.
A short shadow means the Sun is high. A long shadow means the Sun is low.
Let's remember.
Seasons happen because the Earth is tilted.
In summer, the Sun is high, the days are long, and it is warm.
In winter, the Sun is low, the days are short, and it is cold.
And the north and south have opposite seasons.
Sunny work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, nature explorers! Let's visit some extreme places.
This is lesson 6.3: plants and animals adapted to their environments.
An adaptation is a feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat. A polar bear has thick fur and a layer of fat to keep warm, and white fur to hide in the snow.
A camel stores fat in its hump, and has wide feet that do not sink into sand.
A fish has gills to breathe underwater, and fins to swim.
Pause and think. What is an adaptation?
Deserts are hot and very dry. A cactus stores water in its fat, squishy stem.
Instead of big leaves, it has spines, which lose less water and stop thirsty animals eating it.
A fennec fox has huge ears, which let heat escape and keep it cool. Like built-in fans!
Seasons change, so living things must change too. Some animals, like bears, hibernate. They sleep through the winter.
Some birds migrate. They fly to warmer places for the winter.
An Arctic hare grows white fur in winter, and brown fur in summer, to stay hidden.
And many trees drop their leaves in autumn, to save water in winter.
Did you know? The wood frog freezes almost solid in winter. Its heart even stops beating!
Then in spring it thaws out, and hops away as if nothing happened. Amazing!
Your turn. Why do some birds migrate?
Let's test a polar bear adaptation.
Ask an adult to help you make a blubber glove: a bag of cooking fat with another bag inside it, for your hand.
Dip your gloved hand and your bare hand into ice water.
Which hand stays warm for longer? Fat is a great insulator!
Let's remember.
Adaptations help living things survive in their habitats.
Polar animals have thick fur and fat to keep warm.
Desert plants and animals store water and lose heat.
And some animals hibernate, migrate, or change colour with the seasons.
Wild work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, wildlife detectives! Ssh… we're hiding in the jungle.
This is lesson 6.4: adaptations of predators and prey.
A predator hunts other animals for food. A prey animal is hunted.
Predators, like lions, have sharp teeth and claws, and eyes at the front to judge distances.
Prey animals, like zebras, have eyes on the sides of their head, to spot danger all around, and fast legs to run away.
Pause and think. Why do many prey animals have eyes on the sides of their heads?
Many animals use camouflage. That means colours and patterns that help them hide.
A chameleon can change its colour to match its surroundings.
A stick insect looks just like a twig. Can you spot it?
And a tiger's stripes help it hide in tall grass, so it can sneak up on its prey.
Some animals do the opposite. They show off! A tiny poison frog has bright colours that say: don't eat me, I'm poisonous!
Wasps have yellow and black stripes that warn: I sting! These are warning colours.
And a puffer fish puffs itself up like a spiky ball, so it is too big and prickly to swallow.
Did you know? An owl's feathers have soft, fringed edges.
So it can fly almost silently in the dark, and catch a mouse before it hears a thing!
Riddle time! I am green, I am sitting on a leaf, and you cannot see me. What am I?
A camouflaged caterpillar! Did you spot me?
Your turn. Why does a wasp have yellow and black stripes?
Let's play predator and prey.
Cut twenty green and twenty red pieces of wool. These are your worms.
Scatter them on some grass. Your partner is a hungry bird with one minute to collect worms.
Count each colour. Which worms were better camouflaged?
Let's remember.
Predators hunt other animals, and prey animals are hunted.
Predators have sharp teeth, claws and forward-facing eyes.
Prey have eyes on the sides, speed, and camouflage.
And warning colours say: don't eat me!
Wild work, detectives! You have finished the Stage 5 lessons. See you in the practice room!
